subject: Canada lost 42,000 jobs. Rate hike odds rose.
bodyMarkdown:
If you have a mortgage coming up for renewal or you are looking for a first job this fall, Friday moved the odds on both. Canada and the United States published their August jobs numbers on the same morning, and the two reports pointed in opposite directions.

## One border, two labour markets

Statistics Canada reported on Friday that employment fell by 42,000 in August, against forecasts for a gain of about 15,000. The unemployment rate did not budge, holding at 6.4 per cent, which sounds fine until you look underneath. Full-time work fell by 36,000. Private-sector employment dropped by 23,000, and the public sector shed 20,000 positions in its third straight month of declines. Manufacturing added 22,000 and was the only sector with a statistically significant gain. The same morning in Washington, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said American payrolls rose by 162,000 against a Reuters consensus of 56,000, with July revised up to 21,000 and unemployment steady at 4.1 per cent. Douglas Porter of BMO called the Canadian numbers soft but far from a shock after a run of unusually strong months.

## The wage line is the one I would read first

Sitting in the same release is a number that got much less attention. Average hourly wages for permanent employees grew 2.0 per cent from a year earlier, the slowest pace in close to nine years. Canadian headline inflation ran at 3.0 per cent in July, up from 2.8 per cent in June, and the space between those two figures is where the whole argument lives. Gasoline was up 25.7 per cent year over year and did most of the work. Take gasoline out and the index rose 2.2 per cent for the third month in a row. **Core inflation**, the Bank of Canada's median and trim measures that strip out the most volatile prices, averaged 2.0 per cent in July. Underlying prices are at target, wages are decelerating, and the alarming headline is mostly oil.

## So why is a hike on the table

The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent on Wednesday, its seventh hold in a row, and warned that American tariffs, Canadian counter-tariffs and high oil prices could push inflation above 3 per cent. Second-quarter GDP growth of 3.3 per cent gives it room to sound hawkish. By Friday, Canadian rate futures put better than a one-in-four chance on a quarter-point increase at the October 28 meeting, up sharply from Monday, and that pricing came after the jobs miss. In the United States it is starker. Reuters reported on Friday that futures implied about a 60 per cent chance the Fed raises rates this month, with core PCE inflation near 3.3 per cent. Here is where I get off the bus. A rate hike does not produce a barrel of oil and it cannot repeal a tariff. It slows hiring, in a country that just lost 36,000 full-time jobs.

## The takeaway

Two dates now matter more than anything else on the calendar: American CPI on September 11 and the Fed meeting the week after. If the Fed moves, the pressure lands on the loonie and the Bank of Canada's October 28 decision gets harder, whatever the jobs data says. Stop budgeting around a cheaper mortgage renewal, because the market is not pricing one. And if you are job hunting in Ontario this fall, manufacturing was the only part of the economy that grew last month.
